title: Mrs. P. Thomas Agnes Brown Interview, 1960-10-12

blocks.x: On this day...
We are recording today in the home of the late Tom Brown, Thomas P. Brown, at 1220 Magazine Street.
Right on 1228th Street.
At 1228th Street, I'm sorry. And Mrs. Brown has gotten out some of Tom's publicity and photographs and various things.
There is no entries publicity.

He's just got tons of it here. Yes. Pictures all over the place. Various bands he's played with. Well, right in front of me I can see Frisco dancing. And there's Tom in the background playing trombone and on the bass. Ray Lopez it looks like on cornet. On cornet, Ray, yes. And is that Billy Lambert?
That's Billy Lambert on drums.
And the clarinet play I'm not sure of.
Shields.
That's Shields. Larry. Larry.
I think it's Larry or Harry. Larry.
It's Larry would be the one in Chicago. Harry was still young then.
Because I get them mixed up to see.
Those two. And as mentioned in the article in the record changer, Al Capone is holding Tom's trombone case right there. You can see him in the car.
That's correct.
And then, let's see, what does the article say? We once played for a prize fight in Chicago and Al Capone held my trombone case. I have a picture of that.
Which is true.

Now, we have here a little write up that says this script was composed and written June the 3rd, 1955. Let's see, and copyrighted it looks like there too. By Tom Brown, an autographed by good friends. 38 names more on the back, including Tom Brown first, and then Sherwood Manjapan, Edmond Sushan, M.D., Pete Mellom, Mara Menville, Frank Bonin, singer Johnny Wiggs, Bill Lambert, Alfred Lobre, Vincent Varisco. Somebody Brown whose name I can't read. Yes.
Is that FN? Looks like the FN. Oh, uh, Varisco, Vincent. Oh, Vincent Varisco. He played the tom.
Lloyd T. Bacon, Ted Brown, Charles W.R.O.C.H. it looks like, Rock, Roach. Roach. Roach.
Another dear friend of Tom.
Mrs. Catherine Burke. Burke. Raymond Burke. Raymond Burke. Oh, that's Raymond's wife. Yes. Dominic. Dominic. Dominic.
Alamo. Alamo. A-L-A-I-M-O.
Edward Chance. Edward J. I guess that is. Mm-hmm. Joe L.A-I-M-O. Peter. P-A-L-M-A Palamo. Ronald J. Loicano. And Mrs. Lillian.
B-A-U-S it looks like.

Jazz is a big ballahoo today. Would you like to meet the man that started jazz? He's right here in your city standing fast. You shouldn't believe a word of what you've already heard. They're busy telling lies of what they heard. Tom Brown started jazz in Chicago, even built a name for jazz. Jazz was never used to music until Tom, until Brown, I'm sorry, gave it its advance. The colored were not responsible as the great big ballahoo. It was done by the north to kid the south. The colored only played plantation and jazz as a part of swing. You can see how well it has done as they are all having fun, telling what they've done to create jazz. It was started in 1915. Don't be fooled. It wasn't until then everyone has taken copy and claiming that he's the one. The world has misunderstood the correct point of jazz. There's always room for correction for things done in the past. This is the only way I have to get back at them for something wrongfully done. It's too late to derive any benefits. It's let's put it all in song. Give the right where right belongs. I just want my public to know the truth. T.S. Tom Brown took the first band to Chicago. You can see how well it has done. Then down at the bottom, after the signature as it has, Ray did a lot to perfect this jazz. Gus variated to the strain of swing. Arnold played the glorified piano.
G-L-O-F-A-R-E.
Graf-A?
The Graf-A. They call it the Graf-A piano.
Oh, Graf-A piano? No.
What does that mean? Read that. He played the Graf-A. Read it again.
I want to play the G-L-O-F-A-R-E.
That means the Graf-A the piano.
While Bill added tempo to the strain, Tom played a kind of lick here and there to add the beautiful tone. When they were all together, you had the finest jazz in the land.
Now, you read that really good.
Oh, thank you, Ms. Brown.
Now, that would be wonderful. You want that on tape?
Oh, well, we've got it right here.
Oh, yes.

We've got it on tape. Now, here's a, looks like an advertisement. Well, it's a postcard, actually. And it says on it, 1921-1922. Season greetings. A Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year. Compliments of Tom Brown's syncopated novelty orchestra. Now playing unlimited engagement at Vista Garden. It's got a picture of a band. Looks like you've got a band show.
Oh, yeah.
Oh, that's Steve in the background on the band.
Steve in the back, yes.

And Tom is there with a trombone. There's a cornet player, piano player, clarinetist, and a saxophonist. And they have two more saxophones right in front of the trombone and trumpet. Looks like one's an alto and one's a tenor.
See, Tom played big bands plus small bands. And he's got pictures. My God.

Drummer in the background, too. Tom Brown, director, phonograph artist, and composer of Rosa Spain, June, High Yellow Blues, Love Dreams, and others. Earl Corder drums, Abe Friedman piano. Charles Hawk banjo, Ted Brown bass. George Lee saxophone. Joe Caliguri, C-A-L-I-G-U-R-I, cornet. Roy Kramer. That's K-R-E-A-M-E-R.
Kramer.
K-R-E-A-M-E-R. Kramer.
Kramer.
Clarinet, it says.
That's right.
Tom Brown syncopated novelty orchestra. And Earl Corder did this. He dated it 1921. He must have done the drawing. He signed it.
Yes, uh-huh. It was between 21, I guess, and 22. He was a drummer.
And he was a drummer and an artist, too. And a drummer.
Oh, gorgeous.
Mm-hmm.
Sounds funny.

Let's see. Dancers. There is a reason. Tom Brown is back in town, and if you have never danced to Tom Brown's dance music, then you have never danced. If you want to be thrilled again with that intoxicating dance music, don't miss visiting the Vista Garden, 47th Street, near Cottage Grove Avenue, every Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday, Sunday, matinee, and night. The orchestra. Tom Brown himself, the originator of the jazz craze. Abe Friedman plays the piano and is well-known with his music studio. Roy Kramer, clarinet, known for his weird harmony. Joe Gallagher. Gallagher. G-A-L-A-I-G-U-R-I. I don't know how to pronounce that. Known for the laughing cornet.
Paul Crawford, how'd you say? Gallagher.

Gallagher. Oh, Charlie Hawk plays southern harmony on his old banjo. George Lee plays the some-leading saxophone. No, I'm sorry. George Lee plays some-leading saxophone. Ted Brown bass, known for his picking novelty. Earl Carter drums, known as the Tempo Kid. I thank you. That's nice.
Mm-hmm.
And you've got who was in the band. Roy Kramer made some records. Yes. I've heard of him, too. And, of course, naturally, I've heard of Ted and Tom.
Mm-hmm.
Plenty.
Yes.
Let's see.
You read that pretty good.

Thank you very much, Miss Brown. Uh, let's see. In the District Court of the United States for the Northern District of Illinois' Eastern Division, you have Max Hart, Henry Ragus, Dominic James LaRocca, Lawrence Shields, Anthony Sbarro, and Edwin B. Edwards. Sbarro is spelled.
Sbarro. Sbarro. Sbarro.
S-B-A-R-B-A-R-D.
Sbarro. I guess that's Sbarro.

Complainants versus Roger Graham, defendant, state of Illinois' county of Cook. Sbarro. And, uh, that's sworn, let's see, subscribed and sworn to before me this day of September 1917. I guess we can get that from the, uh, court records up there. We can get a copy of this from the court records.
Mm-hmm.
Get that original.
Well, you can have that. I have the original. Oh, we can keep this? I'll give you that.
Oh, we'd love to have this. Then I won't have to read it. You can save my voice.
You can have, you do very good.
Thank you.
You can also have this too.
Oh, that is wonderful. We really appreciate that.
Oh, I got thousands. Oh. You've got plenty left. Yes.
Nah. Uh, this is Ray Miller, Melody King and his black and white Melody Boys, phonograph artist.
They made plenty of records.
There's five of them here. That's a, I recognize Tom right there.
Yes, uh-huh.
And they are wonderful records too. I think I have underneath the Wiley and Skars. That's a very pretty, pretty thing.
Then I come across some of those I don't know.
That's Paul Whiteman's band. Gussie might have been in there.
I was looking for that when I was picking him out today. I don't see Gussie there.
No.
Although he did play with Paul.
He was with him around that time, but it must have been right before or right after.
Probably. So.
So. So. In the early records, there's only six guys there with Ray Miller, Melody King.
Mm-hmm. Well, sometimes I'm quitting. I don't. Just like Mr. going in. The other one drops out. The other one drops in. Isn't that right?

Mm-hmm. Look. Let's see. Now here's another. Looks like a handbill advertising for these tunes. It says, quote, two new hits, please. Hit number one, Rose of Spain. Whoa. Rose of Spain. Rose of Spain. A breezy summer dance and song success now being featured in the stupendous Edwin Carnival.
Mm-hmm.

A rare blossom from the garden of hits. Hit number two. Fred Fisher's sensation. You're the only girl that made me cry. No wonder they, quote, cry, unquote, for more. Try it and you'll, quote, cry, unquote, yet.
Mm-hmm.
That's pretty. A nice thing to have.
I'll give you that, but I think that's the only one that I can find was. He has a grip just packed and stuff.
That might have been a cover of the sheet music or something.
A cover of the sheet music.
Mm-hmm. So let's see. We've got another picture here.
That's Beindorfer.
Mm-hmm. Well, I bet I can tell you who's there. That's Chink. Chink. Chink Martin on the tuba, and he's got a...
Yeah.
Well, it's actually a sousaphone with an upright bell and a string bass in the picture.
Mm-hmm.
And Tom is next to him on trombone. That doesn't look like Johnny. He's put on weight, but Johnny biased off him. Leo Addy is on drums. I recognize him. You do? Now, the banjo I'm not sure about.
Yeah, Loicanna.
Oh, that's Steve Loicanna.
Yes.
And who is the piano player there?
Miller.
Johnny Miller. Johnny Miller.
Mm-hmm.
And Skaggs.
And Skaglione.
Nuncio Skaglione is the name. And in front of the van, let's see. Tom doesn't have any mutes, but yes, he has one straight mute there, I see. Mm-hmm.
Yes.

And then they've got a straight mute for the trumpet, and it looks like one of those old con mutes, huh? Mm-hmm. That used to come with a trumpet sort of pear-shaped. And there's a violin in front of the banjo player. Maybe Loicanna played violin.
Mm-hmm. I suppose so.
And they've got four saxophones in front. It looks like a...
They used to double, I guess. Mm-hmm.
Soprano, alto, C melody, antenna, huh? Mm-hmm.
It's the double.
So...
Tom was the first one that muted a horn.
Uh...

could make them just like that you know. Then after that all come to use.
Steve mentioned that to us too. So we know it's true because his brother Ted or

Billy Bergen. Red Hot we call them.
And let's see over here you have the original band you say. Yeah. Except that Larry Shields was taking Gussie's place. That's right. Correct.
So. So like Gussie said Larry, he's gone two weeks now. He said if they could get down to the root of jazz. Get it straightened out.

They haven't got the root. No it's it's going to be awful hard because so many people tell you different stories. Sure. I know. Well everybody knows that uh certainly Tom thought up a lot of the licks and everything.

You know uh some man told me not long ago they get in arguments in Barons and they fight over Tom. This guy says he wasn't and he says sure I'm sure Tom was the right one. They have arguments. That's funny. Oh. It's ridiculous. Well. Ridiculous is right.
Everybody knows that Tom was playing long before the the people that claimed to have been in it.
Tom was playing before them. You see uh Tom's father was a Browns band too. I've heard that. His father. I guess he taught the boys you know.

And you've got a lot of sheet music around. Oh. I guess some of this belongs to Tom too. All of that's yes. See a fool in love. Till then. Till then. Blue. Blue. Yeah. By uh Grant Clark, Edgar Leslie and Lou Handelman.

You're taking here on your tape recorder.
Well we could all we could all go up to Tulane sometime.

segments.title: Opening at Tom Brown's home on Magazine Street
segments.summary: Recording begins at the home of the late Tom Brown; Mrs. Brown has laid out his publicity and photographs.

segments.title: Photo of Tom's band with Joe Frisco; Al Capone and the trombone case
segments.summary: Identifying musicians in a photograph (Ray Lopez, Billy Lambert, Larry Shields) and confirming the story that Al Capone held Tom's trombone case at a Chicago prize fight.

segments.title: Names autographed on Tom Brown's 1955 script
segments.summary: The interviewer reads the 38 friends' names who autographed Tom's 1955 script, with Mrs. Brown helping on spellings.

segments.title: Tom Brown's written claim to have started jazz in Chicago
segments.summary: A reading of Tom's verse claiming he started jazz in Chicago in 1915 and took the first band there, crediting his bandmates; a spelling puzzle over the 'glorified piano'.

segments.title: 1921-22 Tom Brown's Syncopated Novelty Orchestra at Vista Garden
segments.summary: A Christmas postcard for the orchestra at Vista Garden, with the personnel (Earl Corder, Abe Friedman, Charles Hawk, Ted Brown, George Lee and others).

segments.title: Vista Garden dance advertisement and its musicians
segments.summary: An ad for dancing at Vista Garden near Cottage Grove touts each band member's specialty; Roy Kramer made records.

segments.title: 1917 court document and papers given to Tulane
segments.summary: A September 1917 Illinois court filing naming LaRocca, Shields and others against Roger Graham; Mrs. Brown gives the originals to the interviewer.

segments.title: Ray Miller's Black and White Melody Boys and the Whiteman connection
segments.summary: Photos of Ray Miller's recording band with Tom; discussion of whether Gussie appears and his time with Paul Whiteman.

segments.title: Handbill for 'Rose of Spain' and 'You're the Only Girl'
segments.summary: A handbill advertising two hit songs, probably a sheet music cover.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands and later photographs
segments.title: Photo of Tom with Chink Martin, Steve Loyacano and a New Orleans band
segments.summary: Identifying the band members in a photo and describing their mutes, banjo, violin and doubling saxophones.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands and later photographs
segments.title: Tom as the first to mute a horn, and Ted 'Steve' Brown
segments.summary: Mrs. Brown says Tom was first to mute a horn, making a tin mute, and Teagarden offered a mouthpiece for it; Ted is called Steve.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands and later photographs
segments.title: Hal Stringer's Rhythm Airs and Tom on bass in later years
segments.summary: Looking at a photo of Hal Stringer's band with Tom playing bass and doubling trombone.

segments.title: Hearing Tom at Audubon Park; who really started jazz
segments.summary: The interviewer first heard Tom with Red Hot Bergen; they discuss the original band with Larry Shields replacing Gussie, arguments over who originated jazz, and Tom's father's band.

segments.title: Tom's orchestrations, sheet music and sealed court envelope
segments.summary: Mrs. Brown shows his orchestration books and sheet music, an envelope sealed for court, and mentions being overcharged at city hall.

segments.title: Copying the tape at Tulane and closing
segments.summary: The interviewer proposes taking the tape to Tulane to be copied and kept safely; the recording ends.
